1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6.name: East Indian Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6.background: The Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings files the East Indian Defence under A48, and its Przepiórka Variation (3.g3) under A49. White's Barry Attack, which starts with 3.Nc3, has been tried at grandmaster level by Mark Hebden and Julian Hodgson.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.c4.strategy: Stakes a second pawn in the centre, so White holds more space and Black has to undermine it with timely central breaks. The principal way to meet the fianchetto: the game becomes a struggle over whether White's centre is a strength or a target.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4.name: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4.background: The Irish-American James Mason was the first master-level player to use the London System regularly, including at the strong 1882 Vienna Tournament. The name comes from the London tournament of 1922, where the opening appeared seven times, including in games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4.strategy: Brings the queen's bishop out before e3 closes it in, eyeing e5 and c7. White can use one easy-to-learn set-up against almost anything, but it exerts little influence on Black's half of the board, so Black develops freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: Puts the queen's knight on c3 and prepares Bf4, an active set-up aimed at the kingside and at c7, which a fianchettoed bishop cannot help defend. The knight blocks the c-pawn, so White gives up the c4 lever for speed and attacking chances.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3.name: Indian Defence: Przepiorka Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3.strategy: Meets Black's fianchetto with one of its own and keeps a later c4 in hand, deciding on the central structure only once Black has shown his plans. A flexible, solid set-up that heads for a long manoeuvring game rather than an early attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3.strategy: A modest, solid move: the pawn backs d4 and opens the way for the king's bishop, but it shuts in the queen's bishop. White asks little of Black, who completes the fianchetto and castles undisturbed against a plan of quiet development.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5.name: Torre Attack: Fianchetto Defence
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5.background: The Torre Attack is named after the Mexican grandmaster Carlos Torre, who beat the former world champion Emanuel Lasker with it. Tartakower, Spassky and Petrosian also played it; it is rarely met in modern top-flight play as a primary system but is popular at club level.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5.strategy: Attacks the knight, hoping to trade it or provoke a concession, but the e-pawn guards it and a fianchettoed bishop soon will too, so the pressure is thin. A quiet, low-theory set-up that suits club play and rarely gives White an edge.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling, ignoring the bishop on f4: nothing in White's set-up threatens Black at once. The bishop waits behind its knight, ready to work along the long diagonal when the centre opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 d6.strategy: Builds a compact pawn structure before the bishop moves, controlling e5 and freeing the queen's bishop. The bishop on f4 attacks the pawn, but the c- and e-pawns and the queen guard it, so Black loses nothing and keeps a flexible, solid set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once. With the queen's bishop already on f4, the b2 pawn has no defender, so ...Qb6 can gain time against it; the price is that the bishop on f4 can now trade itself for the knight on b8, which the c-pawn no longer shields.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 d5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn at once, a solid set-up in which the g7 bishop will bear on d4 once the knight moves. It commits the d-pawn before White shows his plan, and the London bishop and knight stand comfortably, so White's set-up is left undisturbed.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3.name: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3.strategy: Props up d4 and the bishop on f4 and opens the diagonal for the king's bishop. This is the London structure: solid and flexible, built to meet any set-up Black chooses rather than to demand something specific of him.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight to c3 instead of the usual d2, where it eyes b5 and the c7 pawn. The fianchettoed bishop does not reach c7, so only the queen guards it against the bishop on f4, and White builds a sharper set-up aimed at Black's queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.Nbd2.strategy: The standard London development: the knight supports a later e4 and leaves the c-pawn free to back up d4. It blocks the queen's file, though, so a quick ...c5 finds d4 guarded by the knight on f3 alone.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6.name: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6.strategy: Builds a compact pawn structure, controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop. Black prepares to castle and to challenge the centre later with a pawn break. The pawn is attacked by the bishop, but the e-pawn and the queen guard it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 O-O.strategy: Castles at once, putting the king behind the fianchettoed bishop before anything else. The d-pawn stays at home, so the central structure is still undecided, and White's quiet e3 has made no threat that needs an answer.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 from the flank before castling. The pawn is held by the queen, the knight and the e-pawn, so nothing is won at once, but with White's queen's bishop already on f4 the b2 pawn is undefended and Black's queen can come to b6 to attack it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Be.name: London System, with Be2
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Be.strategy: Prepares castling without committing the bishop to d3, where against the fianchetto it would meet only the g6 pawn. The favoured square in this line: White gets a compact, flexible position and waits for Black to show his plan.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Bd.name: London System, with Bd3
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Bd.strategy: The usual London square for the bishop, aimed at the kingside, but against the fianchetto it bites only on the g6 pawn, so it has less to do than usual. Sound, and it fits a plan of a knight on e5 backed by pawn and bishop.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.h3.strategy: A useful waiting move: the bishop gets a retreat on h2 if Black attacks it, staying on its diagonal and still covering e5, and Black's queen's bishop can no longer usefully come to g4. It costs a tempo of development, acceptable in a slow game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Be.name: London System, with Be2
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.Be.strategy: Castles, putting the king behind the fianchettoed bishop and finishing the kingside development. Black is ready to open the centre with a pawn break, and White's quiet development has given him no reason to hurry.

Brings the last minor piece out and adds a guard to e5, the square Black's central break needs. The break cannot be played yet, since the d4 pawn, the f3 knight and the f4 bishop all bear on e5, and the knight shuts in the queen's bishop for now.

Challenges d4 from the flank instead of preparing a central break. The pawn is guarded by the e-pawn, the knight and the queen, so Black wins nothing at once, but he gains queenside space and trades a wing pawn for White's centre pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.h3.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once instead of preparing a central break. The pawn is held by the queen, the knight and the e-pawn, so there is no immediate gain, but Black opens the long diagonal for the g7 bishop or gains queenside space.

Castles and ignores h3. The pawn move gives the bishop on f4 a retreat on h2, but it does nothing against Black's set-up, and the king is already safe behind the fianchettoed bishop. Black can choose his central plan once White commits.
Develops the knight to a square where it adds a guard to e5, preparing Black's central break. It shuts in the queen's bishop for now, but h3 has taken g4 from that bishop anyway.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.h3.name: London System, with Be2
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bf4 Bg7 4.e3 d6 5.h3.strategy: Develops the bishop and prepares castling while the queen, the knight and the e-pawn hold d4 comfortably. White keeps the structure solid and leaves Black to decide how to resolve the tension in the centre.

Backs d4 with a pawn, the move the London structure is built around: ...cxd4 can then be answered by recapturing, and White keeps a solid centre. The cost is the b2 pawn, undefended since the bishop left c1, which Black's queen can attack from b6.

Develops the knight to the standard London square, from where it supports e4 and leaves the c-pawn free. It blocks the queen's file, so d4 rests on the e-pawn and the knight on f3 alone, and the undefended b2 pawn is a target for ...Qb6.

Takes at once but gives up the d4 pawn the whole set-up rests on: Black regains the pawn with ...dxc5 or ...Qa5+, and White has traded his centre pawn for Black's c-pawn with nothing in return. Black reaches an easy game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7.strategy: Ignores the bishop: the knight is guarded by the e-pawn and the new bishop, so Bxf6 would only trade a knight for a bishop. Black continues the fianchetto and castles soon, leaving White to show what the early bishop sortie achieves.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 d5.strategy: Grabs the centre first. With the bishop not yet on g7, Bxf6 is answered by ...exf6, which doubles Black's f-pawns in return for the two bishops; otherwise Black has a solid pawn centre and the fianchetto still to come.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop, but leaves f6 guarded only by the e-pawn: Bxf6 exf6 doubles Black's pawns for the bishop pair. A playable, modest set-up that spends a move on a pawn and gives White an easy exchange.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2.strategy: Develops the knight to the square from which it supports a later e4, and leaves the c-pawn free to back up d4. White builds a compact centre with the bishop on g5 keeping Black's knight under watch.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.c3.strategy: Supports d4 with the c-pawn, so the queen keeps its file and ...c5 meets a firmly held pawn. It develops nothing, but the queen's knight can choose its square later while the bishop on g5 keeps its pressure on f6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Bxf6.strategy: Trades the bishop for the knight at once. Black recaptures with the bishop, which gains the bishop pair and an attacker on d4; White has spent two moves with the bishop and given up the piece that made the early sortie worth playing.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 d5.strategy: Stops White's plan of occupying e4 and stakes out the centre with a pawn instead of waiting. The cost: the knight on f6 must keep guarding d5 while the bishop on g5 stays pointed at it, so it cannot move freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 c5.name: Torre Attack: Fianchetto Defence, Euwe Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, and the pawn is guarded only by the knight on f3, because the knight on d2 shuts the queen out. Black fights for the centre from the flank, and the bishop on g5 and the knight on f6 face each other.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 O-O.strategy: Castles and puts the king behind the fianchettoed bishop. Black postpones the central decision until White shows his plan, and the d-pawn keeps its options open.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop. Black lets White build a broad pawn centre with e4 and plans to castle and undermine it with a pawn break, the usual way to play the fianchettoed set-up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 d5 5..strategy: Backs d4 and opens the king's bishop, accepting a slower, closed game now that d5 has stopped e4. White's pieces are well placed for a patient fight, with the bishop on g5 still out in front of the pawn chain.

Backs d4 with the c-pawn and keeps both e3 and e4 available. Black's d5 has stopped e4 for the moment, so White builds up patiently and waits for a chance to undermine d5, with the bishop on g5 still pressing on f6.

Trades at once: Black can recapture with the bishop, which gains the bishop pair and a bishop aimed at d4, held by the f3 knight alone, or with the e-pawn. White gives up the piece that made the early bishop move worth playing for nothing concrete.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 d5 5..name: Queen's Pawn Game: Torre Attack, Grünfeld Variation, Main Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Bg5 Bg7 4.Nbd2 d5 5..strategy: Castles and puts the king behind the fianchettoed bishop. The pawn on d5 holds the centre, so Black can challenge White's from the flank, and a trade of the g5 bishop for the f6 knight would hand Black both bishops.

Challenges d4 from the flank while the pawn on d5 holds the centre. The pawn is guarded by the e-pawn and the knight on f3, so Black wins nothing at once; he gains queenside space and trades a wing pawn for White's centre pawn.
Backs d5 with the c-pawn, the solid set-up of a pawn chain on c6 and d5. It spends a tempo on a pawn move while the king is still in the centre, and the bishop on g5 keeps its pressure on f6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto. White's quiet pawn move asks nothing of Black, who develops by the book and prepares to castle, with the bishop ready for the long diagonal once the centre opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn at once. White's e3 has closed the queen's bishop's diagonal, so there is no pressure to meet, and the fianchettoed bishop can still come to g7 to work on the long diagonal. A solid set-up with a firm pawn on d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop, waiting to place the king's bishop until White shows his plan. It is the modest, flexible form of the fianchetto, and White's quiet e3 gives Black no reason to hurry.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Bd3.strategy: Aims the bishop at the kingside and prepares castling, in a system that supports a later e4 with bishop and knights. Against the fianchetto the bishop meets only the g6 pawn, so the set-up is solid but unambitious and rarely troubles Black.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Be2.strategy: Develops the bishop where it is not aimed at Black's g6 pawn and prepares castling. Against the fianchetto the bishop has little to attack on d3, so e2 is the more useful square, and White keeps a quiet, flexible position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.c4.strategy: Claims space with the c-pawn and puts pawns on c4 and d4, so that White can fight for d5. With the e-pawn on e3 rather than e4 the centre is less ambitious, but the set-up is sound.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Bd3 d6.name: Indian Defence: Colle System, King's Indian Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Bd3 d6.background: The Colle System was popularised in the 1920s by the Belgian master Edgard Colle and developed further by George Koltanowski. It is unfashionable in master play.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Bd3 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop, building the compact structure Black wants. White's slow set-up has to prove it can generate play, while Black prepares to castle and to challenge the centre at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Bd3 O-O.strategy: Castles at once. The bishop on d3 meets only the g6 pawn, so White's attack has little to aim at, and Black can decide the central structure later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.e3 Bg7 4.Bd3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre with a pawn, which White's quiet set-up does nothing to challenge. The g7 bishop will press on d4 along the long diagonal once the knight moves, and White has to find a plan against a firm centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7.strategy: Mirrors White: the bishop completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. Both sides develop along the long diagonals, and Black keeps every plan open until White shows whether he wants to play c4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 d5.strategy: Occupies the centre before White's c-pawn can challenge it. Black gets a firm pawn on d5 and a quiet, solid game, and the fianchettoed bishop will press on d4 once the knight on f6 steps aside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop, leaving the king's bishop for the next move. Black aims at the compact fianchetto set-up and waits to see whether White plays c4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2.strategy: Completes White's fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop is blocked by its own knight on f3 for now, but it will bear on the centre and the queenside along the long diagonal once the position opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.c4.strategy: Adds the c-pawn to the d-pawn to claim space and fight for d5. With the bishop on g2 to come, White's kingside is solidly defended, so Black's usual attack there has little chance, and the game turns on the centre and the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.c3.strategy: Backs d4 with a pawn, but it is passive: it takes c3 from the queen's knight and gives up the fight for d5. Black can develop without being asked any question.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O.strategy: Castles at once, putting the king behind the fianchettoed bishop before White clarifies the centre. A natural, useful move: the middlegame plan is chosen only after White commits his c-pawn.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 d5.strategy: Takes the centre with a pawn while White has not yet played c4. White's bishop on g2 is blocked by its own knight on f3 for now, and Black has a firm centre with the g7 bishop ready to press on d4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 d6.strategy: Controls e5 and frees the queen's bishop before castling, heading for the same compact set-up. A flexible move order that waits to see whether White plays c4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.O.strategy: Mirrors Black: the king is safe behind its bishop and the set-up is symmetrical. White keeps the decisive choice in hand, whether to claim space on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.c.strategy: Puts a flank pawn beside the d4 pawn at once, fighting for d5 and gaining queenside space. The king stays in the centre a move longer, but the result is a solid, slowly manoeuvring game in which White presses on the queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.b.strategy: Plans a second fianchetto, so both bishops aim along the long diagonals at the centre and at Black's queenside. It is sound but slow: the king is still uncastled and Black gets time to claim the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.g3 Bg7 4.Bg2 O-O 5.O.strategy: Stakes the centre at once with a pawn instead of waiting with a quieter pawn move. The pawn takes c4 and e4 under control, and the bishop on g7 gets the long diagonal if the centre opens, so White cannot easily claim the whole centre.

The flexible waiting move: Black controls e5 and keeps a compact pawn structure, with the bishop on g7 free to work on the long diagonal. The centre is left to White for now, and Black plans to attack it from a distance once White shows a plan.

Presses on d4 straight away. White can drive the knight back with d5, which wins space, and the knight then stands on the rim, from where it eyes the queenside squares White weakens. Playable, but it gives White a tempo.
The thematic strike: the c-pawn attacks d5 at once and White fights for the centre with a flank pawn. Black must either support the pawn or exchange it, and the game turns on that struggle.

Develops without blocking the c-pawn and keeps both a central pawn break and a later c4 available. Solid, but the knight on d2 is passive and does not fight for d5, so Black's centre stands without challenge.
Prepares Bb2, so both bishops would work along the long diagonals. It is slower than striking at d5 at once, and Black gets time to firm up the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Stakes the centre at once and keeps e4 from White. The knight on c3 blocks the c-pawn, so White cannot undermine d5 with c4, and the pawn is guarded by the knight and the queen. It is the principal reply: the centre stays Black's before White can build one.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Develops the bishop and invites White to take the centre. If White builds a broad pawn centre, Black gets a flexible, counter-attacking set-up in which the fianchettoed bishop presses on the centre from a distance.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d6.strategy: Keeps the centre compact and waits for White to commit, aiming to attack the white centre later from the flanks. It holds back Black's counterplay longer than the active replies and leaves White free to take space.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.background: Aaron Summerscale wrote A Killer Chess Opening Repertoire, which surveys the Barry Attack and the related 150 Attack, and Niaz Murshed is among its regular practitioners.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4.strategy: The set-up that gives the line its character: the bishop comes out before e3 closes it in and eyes c7, which a fianchettoed bishop cannot help to defend. White gives up flexibility in the centre for speed and attacking chances.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bg5.strategy: Develops the bishop on the other diagonal, pressing on the knight on f6, but it no longer eyes c7, so the attacking sting of the set-up is gone. Black can hit the bishop with the knight at once and gain time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.e3.strategy: Supports d4 and frees the king's bishop, but closes in the queen's bishop behind the pawn chain. A quiet, safe set-up that gives up the idea of getting that bishop out first.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7.strategy: The natural development, preparing castling. It leaves c7 guarded by the queen alone, so Black has to watch for a knight jump to b5 that doubles the attack there and would fork king and rook on c7.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 c6.strategy: Backs the d5 pawn and takes b5 away from White's knight, so the pressure on c7 is dealt with before it starts. A solid choice that keeps the centre firm and leaves the light-squared bishop free to come out.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bf5.strategy: Brings the light-squared bishop out before the pawns close it in, and challenges White's bishop on its own terms. But the knight can attack it from h4, and a jump to b5 piles on c7, so Black has to keep an eye on both.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e.strategy: Protects the bishop on f4 and the d4 pawn and opens the king's bishop. A modest move that makes White's attacking formation safe before anything is launched against the king.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.Q.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Tarzan Attack
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.Q.strategy: Backs the bishop and prepares to trade off the fianchettoed bishop, the key defender of Black's king, with Bh6. The unmoved e-pawn leaves the king's bishop shut in, so White's development lags behind the early attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.h.strategy: Takes g4 away from Black's knight and bishop and gives the bishop on f4 the h2 square as a retreat. A useful precaution, but it spends a tempo on a pawn move while the king's bishop is still shut in and Black develops freely.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e.strategy: Castles, putting the king behind the bishop while the centre stays firm. Black keeps solid and waits to see how White arranges the attack, since nothing on the board forces him to act yet.

Solidifies d5 and takes b5 from the knight before castling, so the pressure on c7 never develops. Black keeps a firm centre and free development for the light-squared bishop, whose exchange is a natural idea.

Brings the light-squared bishop out before the pawn chain closes it in, and tackles the knight on f3 that guards the kingside. Playable, but White gets a free hand for a kingside pawn storm if the bishops are traded.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Barry Attack, Grünfeld Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 g6 3.Nc3 d5 4.Bf4 Bg7 5.e.strategy: Develops the last minor piece and prepares castling, with a knight jump to e5 and a pawn push on the kingside as the attacking ideas behind the set-up.
Prepares to trade off the fianchettoed bishop, Black's main defender of the king, with Bh6. White's king is still in the centre while this goes on, so the plan costs time, and Black meets it calmly.

Develops the bishop on the diagonal towards Black's kingside and guards the e4 square. It is harmless and sound, but less flexible than keeping the bishop at home, and Black can challenge it with a bishop trade.
